title: The Scroll, the Watchman, and the Silent Prophet
summary: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey. God sends him to the house of Israel with a face made as hard as theirs. The Spirit carries him to the exiles at Tel-abib, where he sits overwhelmed for seven days. Then God appoints him a watchman responsible to warn the wicked and the righteous, and finally tells him to shut himself in his house, bound and unable to speak except when God opens his mouth.
story: This chapter completes Ezekiel's call, which began with the vision of God's glory in chapter 1 and the commission in chapter 2. Three things are added. First, the prophet internalizes the message by eating the scroll. Second, he is given a role, that of a watchman, which defines his responsibility to the people. Third, he is given a strange restriction: he will be confined and speechless except when God speaks through him. These three elements shape the rest of the book. The watchman charge is repeated almost word for word in chapter 33, at the turning point when news of Jerusalem's fall arrives, and the silence is lifted at that same moment (33:21-22). Chapters 1 to 3 thus prepare for the whole of Ezekiel's ministry.
historical:
Ezekiel is taken to the exiles at Tel-abib by the River Kebar (verse 15). The name comes from a Babylonian expression meaning a mound of the flood, the word Babylonians used for an ancient ruin mound, a place where an old settlement had been destroyed long before. Deported peoples were often settled on such abandoned sites to rebuild them and farm the surrounding land. The exiles there lived in their own community and had their own elders (8:1; 14:1), but they were subjects of Babylon and far from home.

This was 593 BC, some six or seven years before Jerusalem's final destruction. The exiles still hoped that Jerusalem would stand and that they would return soon. Ezekiel's task was to tell them otherwise, and his message would be unwelcome. The seven days he sat among them overwhelmed (verse 15) may reflect his shock at the vision, his distress at the message he carried, or his identification with the exiles' own grief.
cultural:
Eating the scroll was a vision experience, not a literal meal, but it drew on real images. Honey was the sweetest thing an ancient Israelite knew, and the psalms say God's words are sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:10; 119:103). The sweetness here is the sweetness of receiving God's word, even when the content is lament and woe. The command to make Ezekiel's forehead as hard as flint or diamond (verse 9) plays on the idiom of a hard forehead, meaning stubbornness; God will make his prophet more stubborn than his hearers.

The watchman was a familiar figure in walled towns. He stood on the wall or a tower and warned the city when an enemy approached (2 Samuel 18:24-27; 2 Kings 9:17-20). If he saw danger and failed to sound the alarm, the blood of those who died was on his head. God applies that image to the prophet's task: he must warn the people of the coming judgment, and if he stays silent, he shares the guilt. Sitting in silence for seven days (verse 15) also echoes the customs of mourning, in which friends sat with the bereaved for seven days (Job 2:13), and it recalls the seven days of a priest's ordination (Leviticus 8:33), a fitting parallel for a priest being set apart as a prophet.
literary: The chapter has three sections, each opening with a new movement of the Spirit or a new word. Verses 1 to 15 complete the commission: eating the scroll, the renewed sending, and the Spirit's carrying Ezekiel to Tel-abib amid the rumbling of the living creatures' wings. Verses 16 to 21 are the watchman charge, set out as four cases (a wicked man warned or not warned, a righteous man warned or not warned), written in the style of case law, as in Ezekiel 18 and 33. Verses 22 to 27 bring Ezekiel into the plain, where he sees the glory again and receives the command to be confined and silent. Many details echo chapter 2: the phrase son of man, the rebellious house, whether they listen or refuse, and This is what the Lord GOD says. Verse 12 contains a small textual question: the traditional Hebrew text reads a cry of blessing to the glory of the LORD, while many scholars, by a change of one similar letter, read it as a description of the glory of the LORD rising from its place.

outline.t: Sent to a hard-headed house with a harder face
The Spirit carries him to Tel-abib; seven days overwhelmed
The watchman for the house of Israel
The glory on the plain; shut in and silent

doctrines.note: The prophet must take God's word into himself before he can speak it, and it proves sweet even when its content is judgment. He speaks only when God opens his mouth (verse 27), so that his words are clearly God's and not his own.

The watchman passage makes each person accountable for his own response: the wicked who refuse warning die in their iniquity, and the righteous who turn to evil are not saved by past good deeds (verses 18 to 21). Judgment is personal, not only national.

The prophet is responsible to warn, not to produce results. If he warns and is ignored, he has saved himself; if he stays silent, their blood is on him (verses 18 and 19). The passage has shaped Christian thinking about the duty to speak the truth to others.
The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up, carries him, and sets him on his feet (verses 12, 14, and 24). The prophet's movements and his strength depend on the Spirit of God.

words.note: Tsaphah, to watch, keep watch, look out. The participle means a watchman (verse 17). The watchman's job was to see danger before others did and to sound the alarm. The title defines Ezekiel's role as warning rather than persuading.

Megillah, scroll. The scroll that Ezekiel eats is full of lament and woe, yet it tastes sweet (verse 3). The same image appears in Revelation 10:9-10, where John eats a little scroll that is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach.

Kavod, glory. The glory of the LORD appears again on the plain (verse 23), just as Ezekiel saw it by the River Kebar. It confirms that the vision of chapter 1 was not a one-time event, and it prepares for the glory's movement throughout the book.

christ: The New Testament takes up the image of eating God's word in Revelation 10, where John eats a scroll that is sweet as honey in his mouth, and Jesus says that his food is to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34). The watchman's responsibility to warn is echoed in Paul's words to the Ephesian elders, that he was innocent of the blood of all because he had not shrunk from declaring the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:26-27). But Christ goes beyond the watchman. Ezekiel could warn the wicked and leave their fate to them; Jesus came not only to warn but to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10) and to die for the wicked. And Ezekiel's enforced silence, broken only when God opened his mouth, finds a distant parallel in the silence of Jesus before his accusers, who opened not his mouth though he was the Word himself. These are thematic links, not predictions.

hard.q: Does verse 20 mean that God puts stumbling blocks in front of righteous people, and that they can lose all their righteousness?
hard.a: The verse says that if a righteous man turns from righteousness to iniquity and God puts a stumbling block before him, he will die, and his former righteous acts will not be remembered. Two issues arise. On the stumbling block, many interpreters understand it as the occasion of judgment that God brings on someone who has already chosen evil, rather than a trap to make an innocent person fall; the phrase appears elsewhere in Ezekiel for things that lead to or bring about ruin (7:19; 14:3). On losing righteousness, the passage is addressing the principle of personal responsibility: past good deeds do not buy immunity for present rebellion, and past wickedness does not doom someone who turns. It is not a treatise on the eternal security of believers. Christians who hold that true believers cannot finally fall away read it as a warning that exposes false righteousness, or as speaking of temporal judgment; Christians who hold that believers can fall away read it as a real warning to them. Both agree that the passage calls for perseverance and that God takes the choice between life and death seriously.

questions: Ezekiel's scroll was full of lament, yet it tasted sweet. When has a hard word from God turned out to be good for you?
The watchman is responsible to warn, not to make people listen. Who are you in a position to warn or encourage, and what makes it hard?
Ezekiel sat among the exiles for seven days before he spoke. What might we learn from that about sitting with people in their pain before speaking to them?
